segments.title: Flint Castle on the River Dee
segments.body: The River Dee is broad at high tide and meanders past Flint Castle. Reconstruction images and maps show an outer ward and a protected inner bailey, separated by moats. Water access allows ships to reach the castle. The round corner tower is detached from the inner ward and serves as a keep beside the entrance. Its position combines a final stronghold with fire over the approach.

evidence.note: The castle remains, the River Dee, and the width of the river at full tidal front.
The transcript calls Flint Castle interesting and nearly unique in the UK, then points out the round tower on the map.
The transcript describes the outer ward, inner bailey, ship access, and the separated corner tower that doubles as a keep and covers the entrance.

segments.summary: Flint's unusual plan places a separate great tower beside the entrance, with defended wards and ship access from the tidal River Dee.

segments.title: Flint's drawbridges and fields of fire
segments.body: Flint's strongest tower overlooks the entrance that attackers must use. An assault first has to cross the moat and exposed ground under fire from archers in the keep. A second drawbridge leads into close combat with defenders in the inner area, still within reach of the keep's arrows. Reaching that point leaves another bridge and the tower itself to overcome. The sequence forces attackers to cross each barrier while the keep's defenders can continue firing.

evidence.note: The most secure point also protects the entrance and would fire into the open area attackers had to cross.
A second drawbridge, fighting in the inner area, and a final bridge under fire from the keep.
The assault route as crossing a moat, entering a killing field, fighting close quarters, and reaching the tower that had been shooting throughout.

segments.summary: Successive drawbridges force attackers through open ground and close combat while archers in the great tower keep firing into their route.

segments.title: Flint's builders and protected harbour
segments.body: Flint was built from millstone grit and sandstone. Richard the Engineer began the work, which soon passed to James of St George. James spent seventeen months at Flint before moving to Rhuddlan. The inner ward and outer bailey formed distinct defensive areas, and a wall protected the harbour. Standing on the Welsh shore of the Dee, the castle also helped protect the English shore.

evidence.note: The transcript names millstone grit and sandstone, transfers construction from Richard the Engineer to James of St George, gives James seventeen months at Flint before Rhuddlan, and distinguishes the inner ward from the outer bailey.
The transcript says a defensive wall protected the harbour and that the castle on the Welsh shore protected the English shore.

segments.summary: Richard the Engineer began Flint's construction; James of St George took over for seventeen months before moving to Rhuddlan. A wall protected its harbour.

segments.title: Flint's £6,000 cost and modern comparisons
segments.body: Flint Castle's stated construction cost is £6,000. A cited modern-money equivalent is about £5.4 million. The comparison with equivalent government spending is tentatively put at double or treble that figure. This larger estimate concerns the scale of the state's commitment, and no worked calculation is given to establish it.

evidence.note: The transcript gives a £6,000 building cost, cites a £5.4 million modern equivalent, and tentatively suggests equivalent government spending would be double to treble that figure without providing a calculation.

segments.summary: Flint's stated £6,000 construction cost prompts a tentative comparison between a £5.4 million modern equivalent and a larger burden measured against government spending.

segments.title: Shotwick and cross-Dee relief
segments.body: Flint formed part of a cross-river system with Shotwick Castle on the English shore. Shotwick had been the more important position before Flint was built. Although its importance then declined, it remained Flint's backing or redoubt point during the new castle's early service. A besieger without ships could not easily deal with both banks of the Dee. Leaving Shotwick alone allowed its garrison to reinforce Flint across the river.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces Shotwick Castle on the English shore and says it quickly lost importance after Flint was built.
The transcript calls Shotwick a critical position before and during Flint's early service because it was Flint's redoubt point.
A force besieging Flint also had to account for Shotwick's garrison sending reinforcements.

segments.summary: Flint is paired with Shotwick Castle across the Dee, making any siege harder because another garrison could reinforce the river-side position.

segments.title: Flint's donjon and independent sea supply
segments.body: Flint's enlarged, isolated corner tower serves as its main stronghold, or donjon, an unusual arrangement among British castles. Its walls are described as seven metres thick at the base and five metres above, with entry requiring access to the first floor. A surviving arrow slit illustrates how attackers crossing the bridge towards the inner ward would face fire from behind as well as from openings in the great tower. Reaching the inner ward still left a further drawbridge to the donjon. The tower could receive supplies by sea, giving its defenders a means of holding out separately. This unusually strong arrangement was expensive and depended on Flint's geography, which limited its usefulness as a model for other sites.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the isolated great tower unique in British castles and compares the enlarged isolated corner tower to a donjon.
The transcript describes the stone walls as seven meters thick at the base, five meters above, and says attackers were not getting in below the first floor.
The transcript describes multiple drawbridges, fire from arrow slits, and says the tower could be resupplied by sea.

segments.summary: Flint's detached great tower combines exceptionally thick walls with a separate drawbridge and access to supplies by sea.

segments.title: A wooden gallery for the future Edward II
segments.body: Edward I's son, the future Edward II, visited Flint in 1301 as Prince of Wales. The keep already contained stone floors above one another. A wooden gallery was built above them to provide more space for the visit.

evidence.note: A wooden gallery was built above the tower's stone floors to provide more space during the future Edward II's 1301 visit.

segments.summary: A wooden gallery gave the future Edward II more room in the great tower during his 1301 visit.

segments.title: Edward I's first Ring of Iron castle
segments.body: Flint was the first castle in Edward I's Ring of Iron. Work began in 1277, immediately after the first Welsh war. Edward arrived with his army and announced his intention to build there. The army's presence gave force to that decision, making the new military base an assertion of royal power.

evidence.note: The transcript calls Flint the first castle in the Iron Ring and says Edward I began building there with his army after the first Welsh war in 1277.

segments.summary: Flint began Edward I's Ring of Iron in 1277, with the decision to build backed by the army he brought to the site.

segments.title: Welsh attacks in 1282 and 1294
segments.body: Two early attacks put Flint's defensive system under pressure. Dafydd ap Gruffudd besieged the castle in 1282 but failed to overcome its large killing field. During the 1294 revolt, the castle was threatened again. This time its constable burned the exposed outer area to deny it to the attackers while remaining secure in the stone stronghold. The episodes show the strength of Flint's permanent works and the harsher measures used when a siege reached the site.

evidence.note: The transcript says Dafydd ap Gruffudd besieged Flint in 1282 but did not take the castle.
The transcript says the castle was attacked during the 1294 revolt and that its constable burned the outer area to prevent Welsh capture.

segments.summary: Two Welsh attacks test Flint's defences, with a failed 1282 siege followed by the constable burning vulnerable outer areas during the revolt of 1294.

segments.title: Richard II and the 1647 siege
segments.body: Flint's later history links a medieval succession crisis with the English Civil War. Richard II was held there by Henry Bolingbroke in 1399, giving the castle a place in the transfer of the English crown. Flint then had a comparatively quiet history until Royalists and Parliamentarians contested it in 1647. The resulting siege lasted three months. Roughly 370 years after construction, the castle could still serve as a serious defended position.

evidence.note: The transcript says Richard II was held at Flint by Henry Bolingbroke in 1399.
The transcript describes a three-month siege in 1647 and stresses that the castle remained defensible about 370 years after it was built.

segments.summary: Flint holds Richard II for Henry Bolingbroke in 1399 and remains defensible enough to sustain a three-month Civil War siege in 1647.

segments.title: Flint's later uses and naval namesake
segments.body: By the nineteenth century, Flint Castle's outer bailey formed part of Flintshire's county jail. Quarrying also took place nearby. During the Second World War, Flint gave its name to a Castle-class corvette in Royal Navy service.

evidence.note: The transcript says the outer bailey became part of the county jail, mentions nearby quarrying, and notes a Second World War Castle-class corvette associated with Flint.

segments.summary: Flint's outer bailey became part of Flintshire's county jail, with quarrying nearby. Its naval namesake was a Second World War Castle-class corvette.

segments.title: Why Edward I entered North Wales at Flint
segments.body: The closing plan shows the great tower separated from the inner ward, with a moat and other protections making Flint difficult to attack. The castle was Edward I's first statement of intent at his entry into North Wales. The choice of route is explained by a war against Gwynedd and Snowdonia, rather than a campaign against Wales as a whole. Southern Wales was generally richer and would have been easier for the strength of his forces to reach. His immediate opponents were in the north, so that easier southern approach would not have addressed the same problem. Water access was a major part of the design of this first stronghold in the Ring of Iron.

evidence.note: The transcript returns to a plan showing the great tower separated from the inner ward and emphasizes the moat and other protections.
The transcript says the moat and tower layout made the castle difficult to take and calls Flint a statement of intent.
The transcript says Edward entered Wales here because the problem was northern Wales, Snowdonia, and Gwynedd, and that water was a major part of the design.

segments.summary: Edward I's opponents in Gwynedd and Snowdonia explain the choice of a northern approach, even though southern Wales was richer and easier for his forces to reach.
